questions.q: What specifically makes mean-variance (Markowitz) optimization numerically unstable in practice?
options: It requires too much historical data to even run
It needs to invert the covariance matrix, which becomes unstable when assets are highly correlated
It can only handle two assets at a time
It assumes returns are always positive
questions.explain: Markowitz's optimal weights require inverting the covariance matrix. When assets are highly correlated, the matrix is close to singular and its inverse amplifies small estimation errors into large, unstable weight changes.

questions.q: What is the purpose of the 'quasi-diagonalization' step in HRP?
options: It inverts the covariance matrix using a diagonal approximation
It reorders assets by their hierarchical cluster order so similar assets sit next to each other, without changing any values
It removes all but the diagonal entries of the correlation matrix
It converts returns into z-scores before clustering
questions.explain: Quasi-diagonalization reorders the rows/columns of the correlation matrix according to the clustering tree's leaf order, making the matrix approximately block-diagonal, which sets up the recursive bisection step.

questions.q: In HRP's recursive bisection step, how is weight allocated between two sibling clusters?
options: Equally, 50/50, regardless of risk
Inversely proportional to each cluster's variance — the lower-variance cluster gets more weight
Proportional to the number of assets in each cluster
Based on each cluster's historical average return
questions.explain: Recursive bisection allocates more weight to the sibling cluster with lower variance, following an inverse-variance logic at each split, recursing down until every individual asset has a weight.

questions.q: Does any step of the HRP algorithm as described require inverting the full covariance matrix?
options: Yes, in the tree clustering step
Yes, in the quasi-diagonalization step
No — every allocation decision only compares the variance of one sub-cluster to another
Yes, in the final weight normalization step
questions.explain: HRP's entire allocation logic is built from pairwise variance comparisons between sibling clusters at each level of the tree. No step inverts the full covariance matrix, which is precisely what makes it more stable than Markowitz optimization.

questions.q: According to the lesson, how do HRP portfolios typically compare to Markowitz portfolios in research findings?
options: HRP always has a higher in-sample Sharpe ratio
HRP portfolios don't always win on in-sample Sharpe ratio but tend to be more robust out-of-sample
HRP and Markowitz always produce identical weights
HRP cannot be backtested at all
questions.explain: López de Prado's research found HRP didn't necessarily maximize in-sample Sharpe ratio, but it tended to produce more stable, better-diversified weights that held up better out-of-sample than Markowitz's unstable, inversion-based weights.
